short: An altar carved to make the Augustan peace look like a natural, permanent order.
full:
The Senate commissioned the Ara Pacis Augustae, the Altar of Augustan Peace, on 4 July 13 BCE to mark Augustus's return from three years settling the provinces of Gaul and Hispania. It was consecrated on 30 January 9 BCE, the birthday of his wife Livia. The marble altar stands within a walled enclosure carved in low relief with a procession of the imperial family, priests and magistrates, interwoven with acanthus scrollwork and mythological panels showing Aeneas, Romulus and Remus, and a personification of abundant peace.

Unlike the triumphal art it superseded, the altar shows no battle and no defeated enemy; its argument for the new regime is fertility, ritual continuity and a family visibly at the centre of the state. It stood on the Campus Martius near the Mausoleum of Augustus and the great sundial-obelisk he had erected, forming a single monumental statement about his reign. Fragments were recovered from the sixteenth century onward, and the altar was reassembled and displayed in Rome in 1938.
